citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, Eq. (2) with the sentence ‘As $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}] \propto C^E_{ij}$, controlling for $C^E_{ij}$ ensures that any random deviations in $C_{ij}$ from $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}]$ may be interpreted causally’ (repeated with Eqs. (4) and (6)), and main Methods, ‘As a result, our regression strategy allowed us to estimate the causal effect of the proportion of social referents in the seed group’. The witness is the validators' construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 13–14 (supplement PDF pp. 13–14), repeated at SI pp. 15–16 and in the note to Table S7 (SI p. 42); main p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact design witnessing insufficiency of randomization, an eligible-composition main effect and marginal average linearity alone; the witness violates the preferred qualified response restriction.
[Design] One randomization block of four schools $i = 1,2,3,4$ with eligible-group referent fractions $q_i = C^E_i$, $(q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4) = (\tfrac1{10},\tfrac1{10},\tfrac3{10},\tfrac3{10})$. Each school has 40 seed-eligible students in four strata of 10, and every stratum of school $i$ contains exactly $10q_i$ referents (1 or 3). The set of treated schools is one of the six two-element subsets of $\{1,2,3,4\}$, each with probability $\tfrac16$; $D_i = 1$ if school $i$ is treated and $D_i = 0$ otherwise. Independently of that choice, in each treated school and each stratum 5 of the 10 eligibles are drawn uniformly without replacement, independently across strata and schools; the 20 students drawn are the seeds. For a treated school $C_i = K_i/20$, where $K_i$ is the number of referents among its seeds; for a control school the regressor $C_iD_i$ is $0$.
[Potential outcomes, fixed before both randomizations] $Y_i(0) = \tfrac3{10}$ if school $i$ is a control; $Y_i(1,S) = \tfrac3{10} - q_i$ if it is treated, for every seed set $S$. The observed outcome is $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - D_iq_i$.
Claims.
(i) [The randomization and seed-moment premises hold.] $\Pr(D_i = 1) = \tfrac12$ for each $i$. Given $D_i = 1$, $\mathrm{E}[C_i] = q_i$ (so $\mathrm{E}[C_i] \propto C^E_i$, with constant 1) and $\mathrm{Var}(C_i) = q_i(1-q_i)/36$, that is $\tfrac1{400}$ when $q_i = \tfrac1{10}$ and $\tfrac7{1200}$ when $q_i = \tfrac3{10}$.
(ii) [Composition has no effect, and the average causal curve is linear.] For every school $i$ and all seed sets $S, S'$, $Y_i(1,S) - Y_i(1,S') = 0$. Write $Y_i(1,c)$ for the common value of $Y_i(1,S)$ over the seed sets $S$ of composition $c$. For every $c$ in the common feasible support $\{0, \tfrac1{20}, \tfrac2{20}, \tfrac3{20}, \tfrac4{20}\}$, the average effect of treatment at composition $c$ is $\bar\tau(c) = \tfrac14\sum_{i=1}^{4}[Y_i(1,c) - Y_i(0)] = -\tfrac14\sum_i q_i = -\tfrac15$: linear in $c$, with intercept $-\tfrac15$ and slope $0$.
(iii) [Expected normal equations of regression (2).] Let $M = I_4 - \tfrac14\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'$ (which removes the block effect $\alpha_j$ in each realization), let $X$ be the $4\times3$ matrix with columns $D = (D_i)$, $q = (q_i)$ and $Z = (C_iD_i)$, and let $Y = (Y_i)$. Then
$$G := \mathrm{E}[X'MX] = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & \tfrac15\\ 0 & \tfrac1{25} & \tfrac1{50}\\ \tfrac15 & \tfrac1{50} & \tfrac{151}{2400}\end{pmatrix},\qquad h := \mathrm{E}[X'MY] = \begin{pmatrix}-\tfrac15\\ -\tfrac1{50}\\ -\tfrac{17}{300}\end{pmatrix},$$
$\det G = \tfrac{31}{60000} \ne 0$, and the unique solution of $G\,(\tau_0,\gamma,\beta)' = h$ is $(\tau_0^*,\gamma^*,\beta^*) = (-\tfrac3{31},\,-\tfrac{15}{62},\,-\tfrac{16}{31})$. So the coefficient on $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ is $\beta^* = -\tfrac{16}{31} \ne 0$, while the slope of the causal effect with respect to composition in (ii) is $0$, in every school and on average.
(iv) [Where the coefficient comes from.] In the same design, for outcomes $Y_i = a + \tau D_i + b_1D_i(C_i - q_i) + b_2D_i(q_i - \tfrac15) + g\,q_i$ with constants $a, \tau, b_1, b_2, g$ (the causal composition slope is $b_1$ in every school, and the average causal curve is $\tau + b_1(c - \tfrac15)$), the solution of the expected normal equations of (iii) has $\beta^* = \dfrac{15\,b_1 + 16\,b_2}{31}$, which equals $b_1$ only when $b_1 = b_2$. The witness is $a = \tfrac3{10}$, $\tau = -\tfrac15$, $b_1 = 0$, $b_2 = -1$, $g = 0$.
(v) [Limit; its finite content is (iii).] For $B$ independent copies of this block, the OLS coefficient on $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ in the regression of $Y_{ij}$ on block indicators, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}D_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ converges in probability to $-\tfrac{16}{31}$ as $B \to \infty$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: $Y_{ij}$, $\alpha_j$, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}$, $C^E_{ij}$ and Eq. (2), $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau_0D_{ij} + \beta C_{ij}D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$, fitted by OLS (SI p. 13; transcribed in standing assumption (S3) and in P037-T14); the design, two of four schools treated in each block and half of the seed-eligibles drawn within four blocks (standing assumptions (S1), (S2)); ‘All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups’ (SI p. 6), so the $q_i$ are fixed. Composition is a fraction (standing assumption (S4)). Not in the paper and defined by the validator (P037-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2–5): the potential outcomes $Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1,S)$ of a school (the paper gives the school-level regressions no potential-outcome notation); the average causal curve $\bar\tau(c)$, the paper's ‘average causal effect of treatment at a given composition’; the centring matrix $M$, which profiles out the block effect within each realized block, so that $G$ and $h$ are the expectations of the realized within-block cross-products and not the cross-products of expected regressors; and the expected normal equations $G\,(\tau_0,\gamma,\beta)' = h$, whose solution is the limit in (v). The seed law: in a stratum with $r$ referents the number drawn is hypergeometric, $\Pr(k) = \binom{r}{k}\binom{10-r}{5-k}/\binom{10}{5}$; $K_i$ is the sum of four independent such counts, with values $0,\dots,4$ ($q_i = \tfrac1{10}$) or $0,\dots,12$ ($q_i = \tfrac3{10}$). Collapsing to the pair of treated schools and their two counts gives $5^2 + 4\cdot5\cdot13 + 13^2 = 454$ states, listed with their probabilities in P037-E001/v1/artifact/assignment_states.csv.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Claims (i)–(iv) are exact and finite; only (v) is a limit. (iii) uses the seed law only through (i) and the independence of the two treated schools' draws: $D'MD = 1$ and $q'Mq = \tfrac1{25}$ in every realization; $\mathrm{E}[D'Mq] = 0$; $\mathrm{E}[D'MZ] = \tfrac14\sum_iq_i = \tfrac15$; $\mathrm{E}[q'MZ] = \tfrac12\sum_i(q_i - \tfrac15)q_i = \tfrac1{50}$; with $v_i = \mathrm{Var}(C_i \mid D_i = 1)$ and $\sum_iv_i = \tfrac1{60}$, $\mathrm{E}\sum_iD_iC_i^2 = \tfrac12\sum_i(q_i^2 + v_i) = \tfrac{13}{120}$; with $S = \sum_iD_iq_i \in \{\tfrac15,\tfrac25,\tfrac35\}$ with probabilities $\tfrac16,\tfrac46,\tfrac16$, $\mathrm{E}[S^2] = \tfrac{13}{75}$ and $\mathrm{E}[(\sum_iD_iC_i)^2] = \tfrac{13}{75} + \tfrac1{120} = \tfrac{109}{600}$, so $\mathrm{E}[Z'MZ] = \tfrac{13}{120} - \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{109}{600} = \tfrac{151}{2400}$; $h_D = -\tfrac14\sum_iq_i$, $h_q = -\tfrac12\sum_i(q_i - \tfrac15)q_i$ and $h_Z = -\tfrac12\sum_iq_i^2 + \tfrac14\mathrm{E}[S^2] = -\tfrac1{10} + \tfrac{13}{300}$. Residual form: the projection of $MZ$ on $MD$ and $Mq$ has coefficients $\tfrac15$ and $\tfrac12$, and its residual $r$ has $\mathrm{E}[r'r] = \tfrac{31}{2400}$ and $\mathrm{E}[r'MY] = -\tfrac1{150}$, whose ratio is $-\tfrac{16}{31}$. For (v): the per-block cross-products $X'MX$ and $X'MY$ are bounded and independent and identically distributed across blocks, their averages converge to $G$ and $h$ (law of large numbers), and matrix inversion is continuous at the nonsingular $G$.
canonical_claim.note: A counterexample to identification from randomization, an eligible-composition main effect and marginal average linearity alone. The witness has treatment moderation −q_i and violates the sufficient response restriction of the preferred qualified interaction model; it does not refute that model or establish empirical misspecification.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Expected-equations identification under a response moment condition, and optional centered or augmented regressions
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix pp. 13–14 and 15–16 (supplement PDF pp. 13–16); main p. 568 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Expected-equations identification under an explicitly imposed response moment, together with optional centered or augmented regressions under their own common-slope, fixed-sample, seed-independent-control and positive-variation conditions. The printed specification is not shown to require replacement. Exact schoolwise common treatment intercepts and a linear untreated mean are sufficient special cases, not necessary conditions.
[Mathematical content, from the validators' derivations (v1 sections 6–7, v2 sections 5 and 7; materials, analysis.md, ‘Exact design mean and correction’).] Setting: a finite set of schools partitioned into randomization blocks; $M$ is the within-block centring matrix: $(Mv)_i$ is $v_i$ minus the mean of $v$ over the block of school $i$. Fixed before randomization: the eligible-group fractions $q_i \in [0,1]$, the design means $\mu_i \in [0,1]$ of (DM) and all other school attributes. Random, on a finite probability space: the treatment vector $D = (D_i)$, $D_i \in \{0,1\}$, and, for treated schools, the seed-group fraction $C_i \in [0,1]$. Put $Z_i = D_iC_i$ and $R_i = D_i(C_i - \mu_i)$, so that $Z = D\mu + R$ with $(D\mu)_i = D_i\mu_i$. Hypothesis (R), randomized composition: $\mathrm{E}[R_i \mid D] = 0$ for every school $i$.
(DM) [The design mean of composition.] Let the seed-eligible students of school $i$ form strata $h$ with $N_{ih}$ students of whom $K_{ih}$ are referents, let $n_{ih}$ seeds be drawn uniformly without replacement in stratum $h$, independently across strata and independently of $D$, and let $n_{i\cdot} = \sum_h n_{ih} > 0$. Let $C_i$ be the number of referents among the seeds divided by $n_{i\cdot}$, and $q_i = \sum_h K_{ih}/\sum_h N_{ih}$. Then $\mathrm{E}[C_i \mid D_i = 1] = \mu_i := \dfrac{1}{n_{i\cdot}}\sum_h n_{ih}\dfrac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(C_i \mid D_i = 1) = \dfrac{1}{n_{i\cdot}^2}\sum_h n_{ih}\,\dfrac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}\Big(1 - \dfrac{K_{ih}}{N_{ih}}\Big)\dfrac{N_{ih} - n_{ih}}{N_{ih} - 1}$ (a stratum with $N_{ih} = 1$ contributes $0$), so that (R) holds with this $\mu_i$. If $n_{ih}/N_{ih}$ is the same for every stratum $h$ of school $i$, then $\mu_i = q_i$. In general $\mu_i \ne q_i$: for four strata with $(N_h, K_h, n_h) = (13,2,7),\ (14,1,7),\ (14,0,7),\ (14,0,7)$ one has $q = \tfrac{3}{55}$, $\mu = \tfrac{41}{728}$ and $\mu - q = \tfrac{71}{40040}$.
(A) [Sufficient condition that keeps the printed regression.] Let $X$ be the matrix with columns $D$, $Z$, $q$ (and any fixed covariate columns). If $Y = \alpha + X\vartheta + \varepsilon$ with $\alpha$ constant within blocks and $\mathrm{E}[X'M\varepsilon] = 0$, then $\vartheta$ solves the expected normal equations $\mathrm{E}[X'MX]\,\vartheta = \mathrm{E}[X'MY]$, and it is their only solution when $\mathrm{E}[X'MX]$ is nonsingular. In particular this holds with $\varepsilon = 0$, that is, when the potential outcomes satisfy $Y_i(1,c) - Y_i(0) = \tau_0 + \beta c$ for every school with the same $\tau_0$ and $\beta$ and $Y_i(0) = \alpha_{j(i)} + \gamma q_i$ (plus fixed covariate terms): the conditional mean in Eq. (2) is then correctly specified and the coefficient on $Z$ is $\beta$. This condition is not implied by (R) and linearity of the average causal curve (P037-T1).
(B) [Optional alternative under a common within-school composition slope.] Suppose there are fixed vectors $a = (a_i)$, $t = (t_i)$ and a constant $b$ with $Y_i = a_i + D_it_i + b\,D_iC_i$ for every school and every realization (so $Y_i(0) = a_i$ and $Y_i(1,c) = a_i + t_i + bc$: school-specific baselines and treatment-effect intercepts, arbitrary and possibly related to $q_i$ and $\mu_i$, and one composition slope $b$). Then, under (R):
(B1) $Y_i = a_i + D_i(t_i + b\mu_i) + bR_i$ for every $i$.
(B2) For every vector $V = V(D)$ that is a function of $D$ and of fixed attributes only, $\mathrm{E}[V'R] = 0$; in particular $\mathrm{E}[(MW)'R] = 0$ for every matrix $W = W(D)$ of such columns, and $\mathrm{E}[R'M(a + D(t + b\mu))] = 0$, where $D(t+b\mu)$ has entries $D_i(t_i + b\mu_i)$.
(B3) [Centred regressor.] Let $W = W(D)$ be any matrix whose columns are functions of $D$ and of fixed school attributes (for example $D$, $q$, covariates). If $(\delta,\beta)$ solves the expected normal equations of the regression of $Y$ on block effects, $W$ and $R$, namely $\mathrm{E}[(W,R)'M(W,R)]\,(\delta',\beta)' = \mathrm{E}[(W,R)'MY]$, then $\beta\,\mathrm{E}[R'MR] = b\,\mathrm{E}[R'MR]$; hence $\beta = b$ whenever $\mathrm{E}[R'MR] > 0$.
(B4) [Adding $D_{ij}\mu_{ij}$ to the printed regression.] If one column of $W$ is $D\mu$, then $(\delta,\beta)$ solves the expected normal equations of the regression of $Y$ on block effects, $W$ and $Z$ if and only if $(\delta + \beta e,\ \beta)$ solves those of (B3), where $e$ is the unit vector of the column $D\mu$; hence every solution has $\beta = b$ whenever $\mathrm{E}[R'MR] > 0$.
(B5) [The forms with $C^E$.] If $\mu_i = q_i$ for every school, then $R = D(C - q)$ and $D\mu = Dq$, and (B3), (B4) are the statements for the regressor $D_{ij}(C_{ij} - C^E_{ij})$ and for adding $D_{ij}C^E_{ij}$ to Eq. (2). In general $D_i(C_i - q_i) = R_i + D_i(\mu_i - q_i)$; Sol's correction allows $q$ in place of $\mu$ only when the design implies $\mu = q$, and nothing is claimed here for the forms with $q$ when $\mu_i \ne q_i$ for some school.
(C) [The witness design of P037-T1.] There five of the ten eligibles of every stratum are drawn, so $\mu_i = q_i$, and $\mathrm{E}[R'MR] = \tfrac1{160}$. With $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - D_iq_i$ (so $b = 0$): the expected normal equations with columns $(D, q, DC, Dq)$ have the unique solution $(0, 0, 0, -1)$, and with columns $(D, q, R)$ the unique solution $(-\tfrac15, -\tfrac12, 0)$; both give the true slope $0$, where the printed columns $(D, q, DC)$ give $-\tfrac{16}{31}$. With $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - D_iq_i + \tfrac15D_iC_i$ (so $b = \tfrac15$): the printed columns give $(-\tfrac3{31}, -\tfrac{15}{62}, -\tfrac{49}{155})$, the columns $(D, q, R)$ give $(-\tfrac4{25}, -\tfrac25, \tfrac15)$ and the columns $(D, q, DC, Dq)$ give $(0, 0, \tfrac15, -1)$. With the correctly specified $Y_i = \tfrac3{10} - \tfrac15D_i - \tfrac12q_i + \tfrac15D_iC_i$, as in (A), the printed columns give $(-\tfrac15, -\tfrac12, \tfrac15)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P037-T1: Eq. (2) and its variables (SI p. 13), the design (standing assumptions (S1), (S2)), composition as a fraction ((S4)), the centring matrix $M$ and the expected (profiled) normal equations. Hypothesis (R) is the paper's own premise in exact form: main p. 568, ‘any differences between the proportion of treated seeds who were referents and the proportion of seed-eligibles who were referents are attributable to randomization’, and SI p. 13, ‘$\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}] \propto C^E_{ij}$’; the note to Table S7 calls the control ‘the expected value of the seed group composition in the school (over all possible randomizations)’. The publication describes the seed draw as half of the seed-eligibles, block-randomized within four blocks (standing assumption (S2)); when the same fraction of every stratum is drawn, (DM) gives $\mu_i = q_i$ and (R) holds with $q_i$ in place of $\mu_i$, which was the earlier form of this target. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Notes to Tables S6 and S7, ‘Bayesian bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution’: an event on which normalized independent uniform weights and Bayesian-bootstrap weights have different probabilities (the validator's witness; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix, Table S6 note, p. 41, and Table S7 note, p. 42 (supplement PDF pp. 41–42)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness that the weighting rule described in the two table notes is not the Bayesian bootstrap (the validator's; not in the paper). Let $n \ge 2$ be the number of schools ($n = 56$ for the survey outcomes, $n = 49$ for the disciplinary records). Let $U_1, \dots, U_n$ be independent and uniform on $(0,1)$ and $P_i = U_i/\sum_{j=1}^{n}U_j$ (the described rule, normalized). Let $E_1, \dots, E_n$ be independent with the standard exponential law and $B_i = E_i/\sum_{j=1}^{n}E_j$, so that $(B_1,\dots,B_n)$ has the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law, the law of the Bayesian-bootstrap weights. Let $A = \{p : p_1/(p_1 + p_2) < \tfrac14\}$.
Claims.
(i) $P_1/(P_1+P_2) = U_1/(U_1+U_2)$, and $U_1/(U_1+U_2) < \tfrac14$ if and only if $U_1 < U_2/3$; hence $\Pr(P \in A) = \int_0^1\!\int_0^{v/3}1\,du\,dv = \tfrac16$.
(ii) $B_1/(B_1+B_2) = E_1/(E_1+E_2)$, and $\Pr(B \in A) = \Pr(E_1 < E_2/3) = \int_0^\infty e^{-v}\,(1 - e^{-v/3})\,dv = 1 - \tfrac34 = \tfrac14$.
(iii) $\tfrac16 \ne \tfrac14$ (the difference is $-\tfrac1{12}$), so the law of $(P_1,\dots,P_n)$ is not $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$, for every $n \ge 2$.
(iv) [Normalizing changes nothing.] For a matrix $X$ of full column rank, a vector $y$, positive weights $w$ with $W = \mathrm{diag}(w)$, and $\hat b(w) = (X'WX)^{-1}X'Wy$: $\hat b(cw) = \hat b(w)$ for every $c > 0$. So regressions refitted with the raw weights $U_i$ and with the normalized weights $P_i$ give the same coefficients, and normalizing uniform draws cannot turn their replicates into Bayesian-bootstrap replicates.

The paper does not define ‘Bayesian bootstrap’. The validator's definition (P037-E005/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 2, after Rubin 1981): for $n$ observed units the Bayesian bootstrap puts probability masses $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ on them with $p_i > 0$, $\sum_ip_i = 1$ and $(p_1,\dots,p_n) \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$, the uniform law on the simplex (constant density $(n-1)!$ with respect to $dp_1\cdots dp_{n-1}$); normalized independent standard exponential variables have this law (P037-T5 (b)). The validator reads ‘applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution’ as one independent $U(0,1)$ multiplier per school per replicate, used as a weight in a weighted least-squares refit; ‘independent’ is the usual convention and is not a word of the note.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, both notes] “Bayesian bootstrap standard errors generated using 5,000 replicates, applying weights to each school drawn from the standard uniform distribution.” [Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P037-E005, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “Tables S6 and S7: Independent uniform school weights, even after normalization, are not the Bayesian bootstrap. Establish which rule was used: correct the description if the named law was used; otherwise recompute the affected summaries with that law and justify its use for this design, or accurately name and justify the alternative random-weight procedure. No exact replacement standard errors are supplied.” [Sol's smallest repair, verbatim] “If the described uniform rule was used, rename the three row occurrences “Uniform-weight perturbation SD” and describe independent U(0,1) school multipliers, without calling those dispersions Bayesian-bootstrap SEs. To retain Bayesian-bootstrap summaries, recompute the twelve affected entries using Dirichlet(1,...,1) weights and justify application to the design. If that law was already used, only correct the note to state the actual exponential or uniform-spacing construction.”
[Mathematical content.] Let $n \ge 2$ be the number of schools.
(a) [Definition.] The Bayesian-bootstrap weights for $n$ units are a random vector $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ with $p_i > 0$ and $\sum_ip_i = 1$ almost surely, and the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law: the uniform distribution on the simplex, with constant density $(n-1)!$ with respect to $dp_1\cdots dp_{n-1}$.
(b) [A correct construction.] If $E_1,\dots,E_n$ are independent with density $e^{-x}$ on $(0,\infty)$ and $T = \sum_iE_i$, then $(E_1/T,\dots,E_n/T) \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$. Equivalently, for independent $V_i$ uniform on $(0,1)$, take $E_i = -\log V_i$ (and not $V_i$ itself). The forward map $F:(0,\infty)^n\to\Delta^\circ_{n-1}\times(0,\infty)$, $F(e_1,\dots,e_n)=(e_1/t,\dots,e_{n-1}/t,t)$ with $t=\sum_i e_i$, has absolute Jacobian determinant $t^{-(n-1)}$. Its inverse $H(q,t)=(tq_1,\dots,tq_{n-1},t(1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i))$ has absolute Jacobian determinant $t^{n-1}$. With $p_i=E_i/T$, the joint density of $((p_1,\dots,p_{n-1}),T)$ with respect to $dq_1\cdots dq_{n-1}\,dt$ is $t^{n-1}e^{-t}$ on $\Delta^\circ_{n-1}\times(0,\infty)$ and zero elsewhere, and $\int_0^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}\,dt = (n-1)!$.
(c) [The described rule is a different law.] If $U_1,\dots,U_n$ are independent and uniform on $(0,1)$, then $(U_1/\sum_jU_j,\dots,U_n/\sum_jU_j)$ does not have the $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1)$ law (P037-T4 (i)–(iii)).
(d) [Normalization is immaterial for the refits.] Weighted least-squares coefficients are unchanged when all weights are multiplied by a positive constant (P037-T4 (iv)); so the coefficient replicates computed with the weights $U_i$ are exactly those computed with the normalized uniform weights, whose law, by (c), is not the Bayesian-bootstrap law.

Here $n$ is an integer with $n\ge2$, $\Delta^\circ_{n-1}=\{q\in\mathbb R^{n-1}:q_i>0\ (1\le i<n),\ \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i<1\}$, and $p_n=1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Significance statement, Results (first paragraph) and Discussion: the ‘30%’ reduction in disciplinary reports, corrected to 25% (2018 Correction)
canonical_claim.location: main p. 566 (PDF p. 1), p. 569 (PDF p. 4) and p. 571 (PDF p. 6); 2018 Correction, p. E3598 (correction PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] The four passages are transcribed in P037-T17 and the 2018 Correction in P037-T15. [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N001), verbatim] “Replace 30% with 25% in Abstract, Significance, Results page 569, and Discussion page 571 as the official correction directs. Make Results self-contained by labeling 0.20 as the rounded unadjusted control mean and -0.06 as the rounded adjusted effect, and explaining that 25% uses unrounded adjusted quantities for both effect and baseline. This avoids implying the false equality 0.06/0.20 = 25%.”
[Mathematical content.] The Discussion (p. 571) gives the estimated totals of disciplinary events for the 11,938 students in treatment schools: 2,695 without the intervention and 2,012 with it.
(i) $2695 - 2012 = 683$, and the relative reduction implied by the totals is $\dfrac{2695 - 2012}{2695} = \dfrac{683}{2695}$.
(ii) $\tfrac{49}{200} < \tfrac{683}{2695} < \tfrac{51}{200}$, so the reduction is 25% to the nearest whole percent. It is not 30%: $\tfrac{683}{2695} < \tfrac{59}{200}$, and $\tfrac{683}{2695} = \tfrac3{10}$ would require $10\cdot683 = 3\cdot2695$, whereas $6830 \ne 8085$.
(iii) [Rounding of the totals cannot account for 30%.] If $A \in [2694.5, 2695.5]$ and $B \in [2011.5, 2012.5]$, then $\tfrac{1364}{5389} \le 1 - \tfrac BA \le \tfrac{1368}{5391}$, and both bounds lie strictly between $\tfrac{49}{200}$ and $\tfrac{51}{200}$.
(iv) [Consistency with the printed decrease.] $\tfrac{683}{11938}$ lies in $[\tfrac{11}{200}, \tfrac{13}{200})$, so the decrease per student implied by the totals is $0.06$ to two decimals, the printed value; the control level implied by the totals is $\tfrac{2695}{11938}$, which lies in $(\tfrac{9}{40}, \tfrac{23}{100})$ and so is not the printed $0.20$.
(v) [The original calculation.] $\tfrac{0.06}{0.20} = \tfrac{3/50}{1/5} = \tfrac3{10}$ exactly, so the printed 30% is the ratio of the two rounded printed numbers; and no pair $(e, m)$ with $e \in [0.055, 0.065]$ and $m \in [0.195, 0.205]$ has $e/m$ equal to 25% to the nearest whole percent, because $e/m \ge \tfrac{0.055}{0.205} = \tfrac{11}{41} > \tfrac{51}{200}$. The corrected 25% therefore uses a control mean other than the printed $0.20$ (the Correction: both estimates covariate-adjusted).
(vi) $\tfrac3{10} - \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{20}$, which is one sixth of $\tfrac3{10}$: the correction lowers the reported reduction by five percentage points, one sixth of its original size.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The quantities are the paper's: the control-school mean ‘0.20 times per year’ and the ‘average decrease of 0.06 disciplinary events per student in treatment schools’ (Results, p. 569); the estimated totals 2,695 and 2,012 for ‘the 11,938 students in treatment schools’ (Discussion, p. 571); Table S6, Peer conflict, School level main effect $-0.06$ with standard errors $(0.03)$ (SI p. 41). The 2018 Correction identifies $-0.06$ as ‘the rounded covariate-adjusted estimated average treatment effect’ and $0.20$ as ‘the rounded unadjusted control group mean’, and gives 29% ‘without the rounding error’, 25% ‘using both covariate adjusted estimates’ and 23% ‘using both unadjusted estimates’. The relative reduction for estimated means $\hat\mu_0 > 0$ (control) and $\hat\mu_1$ (treatment) on a common basis is $(\hat\mu_0 - \hat\mu_1)/\hat\mu_0$. Rounding to a whole percent: $x$ rounds to 25% when $\tfrac{49}{200} \le x < \tfrac{51}{200}$ and to 30% when $\tfrac{59}{200} \le x < \tfrac{61}{200}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the display ‘The exposure mapping is:’, third line ($d_{NI}$), as printed: two feasible configurations that satisfy two cases at once (the validator's witnesses; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 17] “The exposure mapping is:
$$f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = \begin{cases} d_C\ (\text{Control exposure}): & (1 - s_i) = 1\\ d_S\ (\text{School exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{z}'\theta_i = 0)s_i = 1\\ d_{NI}\ (\text{Non social referent seed exposure}): & \mathbf{I}((\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i = 0)s_i = 1\\ d_I\ (\text{Social referent seed exposure}): & (1 - z_i)\mathbf{I}((\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i > 0)s_i = 1\\ d_D\ (\text{Direct treatment condition}): & z_i = 1 \end{cases}$$”
[Witnesses.] Write $t_i = \mathbf{z}'\theta_i$ (the number of student $i$'s peers assigned to be seeds) and $r_i = (\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i$ (the number of student $i$'s referent peers assigned to be seeds), so that $s_i, z_i \in \{0,1\}$ and $t_i, r_i$ are integers with $0 \le r_i \le t_i$. The five printed conditions depend on $(s_i, z_i, t_i, r_i)$ only: C: $1 - s_i = 1$; S: $(1 - z_i)\,\mathbf{I}(t_i = 0)\,s_i = 1$; NI: $\mathbf{I}(r_i = 0)\,s_i = 1$; I: $(1 - z_i)\,\mathbf{I}(r_i > 0)\,s_i = 1$; D: $z_i = 1$.
(i) $(s_i, z_i, t_i, r_i) = (1, 0, 0, 0)$, a student in a treated school who is not a seed and none of whose peers is a seed, satisfies both S and NI.
(ii) $(s_i, z_i, t_i, r_i) = (1, 1, 0, 0)$, a seed none of whose peers is a seed, satisfies both NI and D.
(iii) In general every configuration that satisfies S satisfies NI (because $t_i = 0$ forces $r_i = 0$), and every configuration with $s_i = 1$, $z_i = 1$ and $r_i = 0$ satisfies both NI and D.
Hence the five printed cases do not define a function of $(\mathbf{z}, \theta_i)$: on these configurations two different exposures are assigned.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: SI p. 17: “An exposure mapping is a unit-specific function that maps an assignment vector, $\mathbf{z}$, and student-specific traits, $\theta_i$, to the actual exposure that a student receives. Each of the distinct exposures are allowed to give rise to distinct potential outcomes for each student. In this setting, exposure will refer to the student's proximity to referent seeds and nonreferent seeds (we will formalize this shortly). Define $D_i = f(\mathbf{Z},\theta_i)$ such that $\Pr(D_i = d) = \pi_i(d)$. We define the exposure mapping as a function, $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$, such that the parameter, $\theta_i$, equals student $i$'s row in the network adjacency matrix. Further let $\gamma$ be an $N$-length vector denoting referent vs. nonreferent status, so that the $j$th element of $\gamma$ takes on the value 1 if student $j$ has an indegree in the top decile of student $j$'s school, and 0 otherwise. The crossproduct of $z_i$ and $\theta_i$, $\mathbf{z}'\theta_i$, is equal to the number of student $i$'s peers that are assigned to be seeds. Further $(\mathbf{z}\circ\gamma)'\theta_i$ is equal to the number of student $i$'s referent peers that are assigned to be seeds. For convenience, denote $s_i$ as an indicator for whether student $i$'s school has been assigned to be treated.” $\mathbf{I}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function and $\circ$ the entrywise product. Since $\theta_i$ and $\gamma$ have entries in $\{0,1\}$, $0 \le r_i \le t_i$. The verbal definition, main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “(i) students in control schools, (ii) students in treated schools for whom no peers are seeds, (iii) students in treated schools for whom at least one peer is a seed but no seed is a social referent, and (iv) students in treated schools for whom at least one peer is a social referent seed.” Feasibility under the design (validator): a treated school has 20 to 32 seeds and a student names at most 10 peers, so the seeds can all lie outside a student's peers, whether or not that student is a seed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, the simulated exposure probability $\hat\pi_i(d_k)$ (printed twice), corrected: the Monte Carlo frequency of the draws that induce exposure $d_k$
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 18 and p. 14 (supplement PDF pp. 18 and 14)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 18] “This vector tells us the probability of $i$ being subject to each of the possible exposures in $\{d_C, ..., d_D\}$, $\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega}\mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$. Each component probability, $\pi_i(d_k)$, is, by definition, equal to the expected proportion of treatment assignments that induce exposure $d_k$ for student $i$. We can achieve an arbitrarily precise estimate of $\pi_i$ via simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design: $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \mathbf{I}[\frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J} f(\mathbf{z}^J,\theta_i) = d_k]$, where $J$ is the number of simulated random assignments, and $z^J$ denotes the $J$th simulated random assignment vector. Aronow [52] provides details on the rate of convergence of the estimated probabilities. In our study, we use $J = 10,000$ replicates of the administration of treatment assignments to estimate the $\pi_i(d_k)$ values.” [Printed, SI p. 14] The same expression, in the sentence “We achieve an arbitrarily precise estimate of $\pi_i$ via $J = 10,000$ simulated random assignments of $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the experimental design: $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \mathbf{I}[\frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J} f(\mathbf{z}^J,\theta_i) = d_k]$, where $J$ is the number of simulated random assignments, and $z^J$ denotes the $J$th simulated random assignment vector.”
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-E003), verbatim] “$\widehat\pi_i(d_k)=\frac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mathbf I[f(\mathbf z^{\ell},\theta_i)=d_k]$ on both SI pp. 14 and 18.”
[Corrected formula.] $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \dfrac1J\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{z}^{\ell},\theta_i) = d_k]$, where $\mathbf{z}^{\ell}$ denotes the $\ell$th simulated random assignment vector.
[Mathematical content.] Let $\mathbf{Z}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{Z}^{(J)}$ be independent draws from the design (each with the law of $\mathbf{Z}$ on $\Omega$), fix a student $i$ and an exposure $d_k$, and put $X_\ell = \mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{Z}^{(\ell)},\theta_i) = d_k]$ and $\pi = \pi_i(d_k)$.
(i) $\mathrm{E}[X_\ell] = \pi$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_\ell) = \pi(1-\pi)$.
(ii) $\hat\pi_i(d_k) = \frac1J\sum_\ell X_\ell$ has $\mathrm{E}[\hat\pi_i(d_k)] = \pi$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi_i(d_k)) = \pi(1-\pi)/J \le \tfrac1{4J}$; hence $\Pr(|\hat\pi_i(d_k) - \pi| > \varepsilon) \le \tfrac1{4J\varepsilon^2}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, and the estimate becomes arbitrarily precise as $J \to \infty$.
(iii) [The printed expression is a different quantity.] The printed right-hand side takes only the values 0 and 1, and its summand does not depend on the index of summation: with exposures coded as numbers it equals $\mathbf{I}[f(\mathbf{z}^J,\theta_i) = d_k]$, the indicator of the last draw, for every $J$. The validator's example: $J = 2$, exposures of the two draws coded $0$ and $1$, target $d_k = 1$. The corrected frequency is $\tfrac12$; the printed expression is $\mathbf{I}[\tfrac12(1 + 1) = 1] = 1$; and the printed expression with only the superscript $J$ changed to $\ell$ is $\mathbf{I}[\tfrac12(0 + 1) = 1] = 0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, ‘Consistency and asymptotic normality directly follow ... given a growing sequence of independent schools of finite size, as holds by construction given our between-school randomization’: the treatment indicators of two schools in one block are dependent (the validator's computation; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 19 (supplement PDF p. 19); the design is on SI p. 5 and in Fig. S1, SI p. 24
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 19] “Consistency and asymptotic normality directly follow from the law of large numbers and a Lindeberg-type central limit theorem given a growing sequence of independent schools of finite size, as holds by construction given our between-school randomization.”
[Witness.] One block of four schools $A, B, C, D$; the set of treated schools is one of the six two-element subsets, each with probability $\tfrac16$; $T_j$ is the indicator that school $j$ is treated.
(i) $\mathrm{E}[T_A] = \mathrm{E}[T_B] = \tfrac12$ (three of the six allocations treat a given school).
(ii) $\mathrm{E}[T_AT_B] = \tfrac16 \ne \tfrac14 = \mathrm{E}[T_A]\,\mathrm{E}[T_B]$, so $\mathrm{Cov}(T_A, T_B) = -\tfrac1{12}$ and $T_A$, $T_B$ are not independent; the same holds for every pair of distinct schools of the block.
(iii) The control-exposure indicators $1 - T_j$ (a student has exposure $d_C$ exactly when $1 - s_i = 1$) have the same covariance, $\mathrm{Cov}(1 - T_A, 1 - T_B) = -\tfrac1{12}$.
(iv) [Without assuming equal probabilities.] For any joint law of $(T_A, T_B, T_C, T_D) \in \{0,1\}^4$ with $T_A + T_B + T_C + T_D = 2$ always and $\Pr(T_j = 1) = \tfrac12$ for each $j$: $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_jT_j) = 0$, whereas mutually independent indicators with these marginals would have $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_jT_j) = 4\cdot\tfrac14 = 1$; and $\sum_{j \ne k}\mathrm{Cov}(T_j, T_k) = -1$, so at least one pair has negative covariance.
(v) [Blocks are independent.] For two blocks randomized independently in this way, the 36 joint allocations each have probability $\tfrac1{36}$, the product of the two marginal probabilities, and the covariance of the treatment indicators of two schools in different blocks is $0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: SI Appendix, Study design, the size of the seed-eligible group: ‘no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students)’, corrected
canonical_claim.location: SI Appendix p. 6 (supplement PDF p. 6); the related sentence is on main p. 567 (PDF p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, SI p. 6] “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4.” [Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-E008), verbatim] “Replace the upper-cap parenthesis by “schools with at least 550 students”. For explicit endpoints: 40 for size at most 200; 64 for size at least 550; interpolate and round to the nearest multiple of four between them. No required change to the main-text design-intent wording.”
[Mathematical content.] For a school of $n$ students ($n$ a positive integer) let the number of seed-eligible students be
$$e(n) = \begin{cases}40, & n \le 200,\\ 4\cdot\mathrm{round}\!\Big(\dfrac{1}{4}\Big(40 + 24\,\dfrac{n - 200}{350}\Big)\Big), & 200 < n < 550,\\ 64, & n \ge 550,\end{cases}$$
where $\mathrm{round}$ is rounding to the nearest integer.
(i) For an integer $n$ the number $\tfrac14(40 + 24\tfrac{n-200}{350}) = 10 + \tfrac{3(n-200)}{175}$ is never half an odd integer, so no tie rule is needed.
(ii) For every $n$: $40 \le e(n) \le 64$, $e(n)$ is a multiple of 4, and $e$ is nondecreasing.
(iii) [The corrected parenthesis.] $e(n) = 64$ for every $n \ge 550$, and the linear scale $40 + 24\tfrac{n-200}{350}$ equals 40 at $n = 200$ and 64 at $n = 550$.
(iv) [The printed parenthesis fails.] Schools with less than 550 students do not all have 64 seed-eligible students: $e(100) = 40$, $e(200) = 40$ and $e(375) = 52$. Exactly, $e(n) = 64$ if and only if $n \ge 521$.
(v) [The share is not constant.] $e(n)/n$ equals $\tfrac25$, $\tfrac15$, $\tfrac{52}{375}$, $\tfrac{64}{550}$ and $\tfrac{64}{715}$ at $n = 100, 200, 375, 550, 715$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $a_i$ is a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure (SI p. 6); the seed-eligible students of a school are those from whom the seeds are drawn (standing assumption (S2)). The function $e$ is the rule of the two printed sentences with Sol's endpoints (‘40 for size at most 200; 64 for size at least 550; interpolate and round to the nearest multiple of four between them’); the paper does not give it a symbol. Main p. 567: the seed-eligible group was ‘designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students’. Table S1 (SI p. 36) has a block whose mean school size is 715.00, so schools above 550 students occur.
canonical_claim.note: P037-E008 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): a misprint in the parenthesis that says where the cap of 64 is reached. Sol's verdict is confirmed in part (batch validation); evidence type recalculation_from_source, so there is no counterexample target; the values in (iv) and (v) are those of P037-B01/work/checks.py. Repair cost: none. A marginal target: a slip in the prose description of a design rule, included because the rule is an explicit piecewise formula, the printed range is false for it and the author's instruction covers every confirmed mathematical error at any severity. Sol's repair names ‘at least 550’ as the range where the cap applies by rule; (iv) records that, after rounding to the nearest 4, the value 64 is already reached from $n = 521$. Not established: any error in the eligible groups actually formed, and the school-average share of about 15% (the roster data are not staged); Sol finds no defect in the main text's ‘designed to represent 15%’ read as a design aim. (i)–(v) were recomputed for $1 \le n < 1000$ when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results, second paragraph: ‘each student was disciplined on average 0.08 times during the year’ when 20% of the group are social referent seeds, corrected to about 0.095
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4), with Fig. 2D on the same page; SI Table S7, p. 42 (supplement PDF p. 42)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, main p. 569] “When 20% of a treatment school's anticonflict group is composed of social referent seeds (proportions ranged from 0 to 37%), we estimate that each student was disciplined on average 0.08 times during the year, a reduction of 60% compared with control schools and twice the average effect of the anticonflict groups.” [Printed, Table S7, column Peer conflict] School effect with 0% Social Referents: $0.04$; Interaction: Proportion of Referents in Treatment group: $-0.85$.
[Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P037-N010), verbatim] “Replace ‘on average 0.08 times’ at 20% referents with ‘on average about 0.095 times’ (or about 0.10 to two decimals), using Figure 2D's adjusted predictions. A clearer complete description uses about 0.223 for the fitted control level, about 57% for the reduction, and roughly 2.2 times the average decrease. In the amended first paragraph, label 0.20 as unadjusted and state that 25% uses an adjusted control mean about 0.226; retain the corrected 25%.”
[Mathematical content.] In the interaction model (SI Eqs. (4), (6)) the estimated effect of treatment at seed-group fraction $c$ is $\Delta(c) = \hat\tau_0 + \hat\beta c$, and the predicted level in a treatment school is $m_1(c) = m_0 + \Delta(c)$, where $m_0$ is the fitted control level.
(i) With the printed coefficients, $\Delta(0.20) = 0.04 + (-0.85)(0.20) = -\tfrac{13}{100}$.
(ii) [Allowing for two-decimal rounding of the coefficients.] If $\hat\tau_0 \in [0.035, 0.045]$ and $\hat\beta \in [-0.855, -0.845]$, then $\Delta(0.20) \in [-0.136, -0.124]$.
(iii) [Hypothesis read from Fig. 2D: the fitted control level satisfies $m_0 \in [0.222, 0.223]$.] Then $m_1(0.20) \in [0.086, 0.099]$. A number printed as $0.08$ to two decimals lies in $[0.075, 0.085]$, and $0.086 > 0.085$; so the printed $0.08$ is not the model's predicted level at 20%, and $0.095$ lies in $[0.086, 0.099]$.
(iv) [The printed numbers among themselves.] $(0.20 - 0.08)/0.20 = \tfrac35$ exactly, the printed 60% with the printed control mean $0.20$.
(v) [The printed 60% is not refuted.] Under (ii) and the hypothesis of (iii), the relative reduction $-\Delta(0.20)/m_0$ lies in $[\tfrac{124}{223}, \tfrac{68}{111}]$, an interval that contains both $0.57$ and $0.60$.

canonical_claim.note: P037-N010 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). Sol's verdict is confirmed in part, upheld on re-run; evidence type recalculation_from_source, so there is no counterexample target. Repair cost: none. A marginal target: a finding about a reported number, included because the number is a prediction of the paper's own fitted model, the correction changes that constant, and the comparison is exact interval arithmetic on Table S7's printed coefficients. What a Lean proof can certify: (i), (ii), the implications in (iii) and (v), and (iv). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, ‘As a result, our regression strategy allowed us to estimate the causal effect of the proportion of social referents in the seed group’, with SI Appendix Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), its interpretation, and Eq. (6), as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); SI Appendix pp. 13–14 and 15–16 (supplement PDF pp. 13–16); Table S7 note, SI p. 42
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 568] “To characterize effect heterogeneity with respect to the seed group composition (i.e., the proportion of seeds who are social referents, which varies from school to school), we use linear regression interacting school-level treatment with seed group composition and controlling for the proportion of students in the seed group who were social referents. Although there was heterogeneity across schools in the proportion of seed-eligible students who were social referents, any differences between the proportion of treated seeds who were referents and the proportion of seed-eligibles who were referents are attributable to randomization. As a result, our regression strategy allowed us to estimate the causal effect of the proportion of social referents in the seed group on school-wide conflict and other outcomes. Accordingly, we can make comparisons between average potential outcomes in, for example, treated schools where seed groups had 20% social referents to control schools, or even to treated schools where seed groups had 10% social referents.”
[SI pp. 13–14] “To characterize how the seed group's composition (i.e., percentage of referents) affects the efficacy of the program, we also use an interaction model.
$$Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau_0D_{ij} + \beta C_{ij}D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}. \qquad (2)$$
Here, assuming that the linear approximation for causal effect heterogeneity is valid, $\tau_0$ is the average causal effect of treatment when the composition of the seed group is 0% referents and $\beta$ represents the slope of the average causal effect with respect to group composition in percentage points (i.e., assuming that the slope is constant, the average causal effect of treatment at a given composition $c\%$ is $\tau_0 + \beta c$.) As $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}] \propto C^E_{ij}$, controlling for $C^E_{ij}$ ensures that any random deviations in $C_{ij}$ from $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}]$ may be interpreted causally. For both models, we also use pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$) to improve efficiency by including them as linear controls in the regression model.”
[SI pp. 15–16] Eq. (4) repeats Eq. (2) and the two sentences that follow it (with ‘(I.e., assuming that the slope is constant, ... is $\tau_0 + \beta c$.)’ printed as a sentence of its own). “We also use covariates to adjust our interaction model:
$$Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau_0D_{ij} + \beta C_{ij}D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}. \qquad (6)$$
Interpretation of the causal effects proceed as above; inclusion of covariates is solely for efficiency improvement.”
[Table S7 note, SI p. 42] “Regression-based estimates of the effects of treatment conditional on the proportion of social referent seeds in the group, under a linear approximation.” ... “Estimates computed using ordinary least squares with covariate controls and fixed effects for randomization block. A control is also included for the expected value of the seed group composition in the school (over all possible randomizations).”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $Y_{ij}$, $\alpha_j$, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}$, $C^E_{ij}$, $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ as defined on SI pp. 13 and 16 (standing assumption (S3)); the design (standing assumptions (S1), (S2)); ‘All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups’ (SI p. 6). The paper does not define ‘the linear approximation for causal effect heterogeneity’, gives the school-level outcomes no potential-outcome notation, and does not say with respect to what $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}]$ is taken (the Table S7 note: ‘over all possible randomizations’). The results that rest on this passage: Table S7 (peer conflict: $0.04$ with robust SE $0.07$; interaction $-0.85$ with robust SE $0.46$), Fig. 2 with ‘($P$ = 0.07, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test)’, the 20% projection of Results, p. 569 (P037-T13), the abstract's ‘The effect was stronger when the seed group contained more “social referent” students’ (p. 566) and the Discussion's ‘future interventions would do well to use as many social referents in their intervention group as possible’ (p. 571).
canonical_claim.note: The printed interaction interpretation expressly carries the validity qualification. The preferred reading is a conditional average causal response with sufficient residual mean or orthogonality; no universal design-alone identification claim is attributed to the paper. The interpretive passage remains not_applicable as a separate theorem.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results, first paragraph (‘the treatment significantly reduced ... ($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test)’), and the last sentence of the 2018 Correction (‘remain statistically insignificant at the $\alpha$=0.05 level’), as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4); 2018 Correction, p. E3598 (correction PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 569, Results] “We first turn to the question of school climate, as measured by schools' overall levels of norms and conflict behavior. Figs. 1 and 2 reveal that the treatment significantly reduced average levels of disciplinary reports of peer conflict in treatment compared with control schools ($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test). In a control school, we estimated that each student in the school was officially disciplined for peer conflict on average 0.20 times per year. We estimated an average decrease of 0.06 disciplinary events per student in treatment schools, a 30% reduction in peer conflict reports.”
[2018 Correction, p. E3598] “The authors wish to note the following: “We reported an estimated 30% decrease in administrative reports of conflict and would like to correct this estimate to 25%. The original paper reported this estimate as the rounded covariate-adjusted estimated average treatment effect ($-0.06$) divided by the rounded unadjusted control group mean (0.20). Without the rounding error, the original estimate is 29%. Using both covariate adjusted estimates, we have an estimate of 25%. Using both unadjusted estimates, we have an estimate of 23%. The original estimate of 30% was reported in the Abstract (line 11), the Significance Statement (line 8), in the results on page 569 (left column, first paragraph, line 9), and in the discussion on page 571 (left column, first paragraph, line 6). In each of these places, we would like to replace the number 30 with 25. The estimated overall effects on administrative reports of conflict remain statistically insignificant at the $\alpha$=0.05 level.””
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The test and the estimate are those of P037-T3: the school-level main effect $\tau$ of SI Eq. (5), estimated by OLS with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and referred to a normal approximation (main p. 568; SI p. 13); Table S6, Peer conflict: School level main effect $-0.06$, Heteroskedasticity Robust SE $(0.03)$ (SI p. 41). The Correction describes no new coefficient, standard error, test or threshold.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N008 (Major) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The two sentences are empirical reports of a test, not mathematical statements; their only formal content is that, read as reports of the same test, they assert $p < \tfrac1{20}$ and $p \ge \tfrac1{20}$, which no real number satisfies (P037-T3 (i)). Lean cannot decide which sentence is wrong: Sol's falsity flags refer to the pair, and neither sentence is shown false by itself. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T3 (i), not_applicable is the right status. The percentage in the same passages is P037-T6 and P037-T17.
